name: Sara Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara, 58, lead developer at a small tech company that builds library-loan software. I have a master's degree and know the lending rules well, though this firm pays less than most senior jobs and there are few similar employers nearby. I use AI every day for anonymous test drafts, but the librarian's branch log decides a disputed fee. My partner drives a school bus part-time, our children are grown, and we rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the librarians a return is not late when the overnight drop box was closed by a power cut. I lead software work for a tech company's library-loan app and use AI every day to draft tests, then check the receipt against the branch log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI stays small, I worry about our bills. I have a master's degree and lead a good team, but this small firm's senior pay is low for the job; my partner drives a school bus part-time, we rent, and only three weeks of expenses are saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing disputed return dates with the branch log and testing AI drafts on old anonymised loans. We'd cancel the 26 monthly video package and put its fee into a rent buffer whenever both wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary money, though I like the work. A parent should not owe a fine because our screen missed the drop-box closure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What showed the drop box was closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: During a storm the book slot was shut for two days, but the app charged late fees anyway. The librarian's sign on the door gave me the right dates for a correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have rents and careers of their own. I want their visits, not their wages in our household calculation.

I'd keep **wrong late fees** visible to librarians and borrowers.
think: I have **three weeks saved** despite leading the team.
I earn **below typical senior pay** and rely on part-time bus income.
do: Keep **reviewing late-fee disputes** against branch logs and anonymous AI test drafts.
Cancel **video package** and save its 26 fee whenever both wages arrive.
feel: **Anxious** about rent despite modest AI change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could code loans and answer borrowers fast, but it should not erase a librarian's decision to waive a wrong fee. I want staff and borrowers in the test, not just developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose lead hours if the firm combines teams, even though I know this system well. Three weeks saved is not enough to absorb a quiet pay cut while my partner's bus rota changes each school term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the library staff group and our union branch in a joint request for monthly wrong-fee figures and a written staffing plan. If the product manager approves a four-week trial on anonymous closed-drop-box cases with librarians checking every reversal, I'd run it; we'd defer the planned replacement refrigerator until paid hours are settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, but I can run a test that a librarian can challenge. The worst metric would call every waived fine a lost sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What cases must the trial distinguish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The storm closure must be in the trial, along with a book returned on time through the open slot. If AI flags both as late, it has not learned the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group send?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The librarians and union reps would sign one letter and request a dated answer from management. That gives the branch workers a place in the decision instead of an invitation to a demo.

I'd protect **librarian waiver authority** before automating replies.
think: I could lose **lead paid hours** even with deep system knowledge.
I cannot cover **a pay cut** with three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write library code before shelf-handling robots arrive around 2031. Borrowers will still need someone to correct a false fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company could cut my lead job when cheaper systems handle both code and tests. My partner's bus wages cannot cover rent and food alone, and three weeks saved is too little for a slow search in a town with few similar jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the regional library network and two local tech firms about actual paid loan-data or software-support vacancies, wages and hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose pay with my partner's actual bus shifts covers rent, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek any available paid local work and contact the landlord before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Being good at a system does not oblige another employer to hire me when its own staff face the same change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show an anonymised storm-closure case and the fee reversal, with borrower details removed. It shows that a signed branch closure matters more than a convenient due date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would school-term hours matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner needs to see the school-term hours in the new job offer. If the new role clashes with paid bus runs, the remaining household pay still has to meet the rent.

I'd check **real paid vacancies** before claiming another career.
think: I expect **my lead job** could be cut quickly.
I cannot cover **rent and food** on school-bus wages alone.
do: Ask **library network** and two firms about real paid loan-data and support openings.

fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches library code before 2031 shelf robots.

steps.text: Ask library network and two firms about paid loan-data and support vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives library staff time to set out which borrower records need a human correction before thinking AI arrives. Shelf robots follow around 2034, after the code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lead a paid records-audit team if the network funds one, but I cannot treat a public meeting as a paycheck. I will be 63 then and have no verified retirement amount that would cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the storm-closure audit file and ask the network for written duties and pay for a borrower-records auditor. If a real paid vacancy opens at hours and wages that with my partner's actual bus shifts cover rent, food and travel, I'd apply; after 2031 I'd take only a signed offer with authority to correct fees, otherwise keep paid development while offered and seek local paid work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether the role will exist, but time lets us ask for the job rather than imagine it. A library can invite my opinion for free while my landlord wants money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the auditor be allowed to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The auditor would need to compare a branch closure notice with a due date and reverse a charge where the record is wrong. I would want that authority in the job description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which income period matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would check both the term-time bus rota and the offered auditor hours. We need actual monthly income, not a full-year salary divided by twelve if school breaks are unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 may take me to 68, but thinking AI will still reach library software before robots move books around 2039. A borrower needs a way to correct a fee long after the coder retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still have three weeks saved now and my partner's bus shifts are term-based. I cannot call retirement secure until both statements show actual amounts and start dates beside our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the false-fine audit and save the cancelled 26 video fee whenever both wages arrive, then request both retirement statements and compare them with a full school-year of bus pay and rent. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if verified income covers rent, food and travel; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid work, without budgeting our grown children's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present rent even with a long lead. I want a real amount on paper, not a retirement story told over a family dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave in the audit file?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The audit file would show the storm closure, return date and refunded amount with borrower names removed. Another worker should be able to understand the correction without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children can visit whenever they like. They have their own wages and rent, and those numbers are not mine to spend.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the lead wage could disappear before the library network hires a paid auditor. Written cut notice, real vacancies with term-time pay and a landlord conversation before rent is late would help us act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a wrong fine is too small to matter. A library fine is still somebody's grocery money, and a fast automatic answer cannot return it by itself.

headlineQuote: A library fine is still somebody's grocery money, and a fast automatic answer cannot return it by itself.
portrait: Sara, **58**, leads library-loan software after a master's degree and checks AI test drafts against librarian closure logs.
Her **lower senior pay**, partner's term-time bus shifts, three-week reserve and few local employers make rent precarious today.
She uses AI **daily** but joins librarians and union coworkers to request wrong-fee counts and staffing terms together.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; a records-auditor move needs a funded paid vacancy, correction authority and wages covering rent.
She will **verify retirement income** against a full year of bus pay and will not assume grown children's earnings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead wage before a paid library audit post exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real term-time pay and early landlord contact would help protect rent.
